# Thyroid nodules

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Endocrinology > Thyroid and parathyroid gland disorders > Thyroid nodules*

[Original Article Link](/library/ao0Q0S)

---

## Summary

<u>Thyroid</u> <u>nodules</u> are abnormal growths within the <u>thyroid gland</u>. They are present in approximately 50% of the general population but only palpable in 5–10% of the population. They are more common in women, especially in <u>iodine</u>-deficient regions, and their <u>incidence</u> increases with age. <u>Thyroid</u> <u>nodules</u> are the clinical manifestation of various underlying <u>thyroid diseases</u>. The majority of them are benign (∼ 95%), with colloid cysts, follicular <u>adenomas</u>, and <u>Hashimoto thyroiditis</u> being the most common causes. Approximately 5% of <u>thyroid</u> <u>nodules</u> are malignant, with <u>papillary</u> <u>carcinoma</u> being the most common form of malignant disease. A <u>thyroid incidentaloma</u> is a <u>nodule</u> that is discovered during imaging for an unrelated cause and should be evaluated in the same way as other <u>nodules</u>. The initial evaluation of all <u>thyroid</u> <u>nodules</u> includes a <u>TSH</u> assay and <u>thyroid ultrasound</u>. <u>Sonographic signs of thyroid cancer</u> should be further evaluated with <u>fine-needle aspiration cytology</u> (<u>FNAC</u>). Identification of a follicular <u>neoplasm</u> on <u>FNAC</u> necessitates further diagnostic evaluation with either molecular testing or surgical excision and <u>histopathology</u> because <u>cytology</u> cannot reliably distinguish between a <u>follicular adenoma</u> and a <u>follicular carcinoma</u>. A <u>radioiodine uptake</u> scan (<u>thyroid scintigraphy</u>) is used to evaluate <u>nodules</u> in patients with low <u>TSH</u> levels. Based on their <u>iodine</u> uptake on <u>radioiodine</u> scans, <u>thyroid</u> <u>nodules</u> can be categorized as autonomous/hot (increased uptake) or nonfunctional/cold (decreased uptake). The most common <u>hot nodules</u> are toxic <u>adenomas</u> and dominant <u>nodules</u> of <u>toxic multinodular goiters</u>. With a 5–15% risk of <u>malignancy</u>, <u>cold nodules</u> are clinically significant. Treatment depends on the underlying etiology and includes, e.g., <u>surgery</u> (<u>thyroidectomy</u>) for malignant and autonomous <u>nodules</u>, <u>aspiration</u> for <u>thyroid cysts</u>, and observation for small, benign <u>nodules</u>.

---

## Epidemiology

* Sex: <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u> (4:1)

* <u>Incidence</u>: increases with age [[1]](/library/h3YcRK)

* Geographic distribution: most common in inland regions without <u>iodine</u> fortification programs, where <u>iodine</u> content in food and water is low





References:[[2]](/library/_905JR)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

### Benign <u>thyroid</u> <u>nodules</u> (∼ 95% of cases)




* <u>Thyroid adenomas</u>

* <u>Follicular adenoma</u> (most common)

* Hürthle cell <u>adenoma</u>

* <u>Toxic adenoma</u>

* <u>Papillary</u> <u>adenoma</u> (least common)

* <u>Thyroid cysts</u>

* Dominant <u>nodules</u> of multinodular <u>goiters</u>

* <u>Hashimoto thyroiditis</u>





### Malignant <u>thyroid</u> <u>nodules</u> (∼ 5% of cases)




* Types

* <u>Thyroid carcinoma</u>

* <u>Thyroid</u> <u>lymphoma</u>

* <u>Metastatic</u> cancer from <u>breast</u>/renal <u>carcinoma</u> (rare)

* Red flags for thyroid cancer ;  [[3]](/library/70X4h9)[[4]](/library/scXtdC)[[5]](/library/zSXrXB)

* Patient characteristics

* Male sex

* Age: < 14 years or  > 70 years [[3]](/library/70X4h9)

* History of radiation to the head or neck

* <u>Family history</u> of:

* <u>MEN2</u> syndrome

* Differentiated <u>thyroid cancer</u> (i.e., <u>papillary</u>, follicular, or <u>medullary thyroid cancer</u>)

* <u>Gardner syndrome</u>

* Symptoms

* Rapid growth of <u>thyroid</u> <u>nodule</u>

* Recent onset of persistent <u>hoarseness</u>, <u>dysphagia</u>, or <u>dyspnea</u>

* Palpatory findings

* Firm or hard <u>nodule</u>

* Fixed <u>nodule</u>

* <u>Cervical lymphadenopathy</u>





> [!TIP]
> In addition to <u>red flags for thyroid cancer</u>, a solid <u>nodule</u> on <u>thyroid ultrasound</u> or a <u>cold nodule</u> on <u>thyroid scintigraphy</u> should raise suspicion for <u>thyroid cancer</u>.

---

## Diagnostics

### Approach [[3]](/library/70X4h9)[[6]](/library/Um0bUg)[[7]](/library/5XXiA9)




* All <u>thyroid</u> <u>nodules</u> (including <u>thyroid incidentalomas</u>) should be evaluated for <u>malignancy</u>. [[8]](/library/-TXDtx)

* Initial tests in all patients: <u>TSH</u> levels and <u>thyroid ultrasound</u> [[9]](/library/Dgb1xG)

* Subsequent tests

* <u>Thyroid scintigraphy</u> for patients with low <u>TSH</u>

* <u>Cytology</u> if <u>ultrasound</u> examination shows <u>indications for FNAC in thyroid nodules</u>

* Additional tests

* <u>Diagnostic workup of hyperthyroidism</u> or <u>hypothyroidism</u> (e.g., fT4, total T3, <u>thyroid antibodies</u>)

* <u>Thyroid cancer tumor markers</u> (e.g., serum <u>calcitonin</u> for suspected medullary <u>carcinoma</u>) [[3]](/library/70X4h9)





![Evaluation of thyroid nodule](media/nsln4lrsgh785aaqrcz9xbxj.jpg)

Evaluation of thyroid nodule




### Initial evaluation [[3]](/library/70X4h9)[[6]](/library/Um0bUg)[[9]](/library/Dgb1xG)




* Serum <u>TSH</u>: may be normal, elevated, or low 

* Elevated <u>TSH</u>: associated with a higher risk of <u>malignancy</u> in <u>thyroid</u> <u>nodules</u>

* Low <u>TSH</u>: indication for <u>thyroid scintigraphy</u>

* <u>Thyroid ultrasound</u>:

* Indicated in patients with palpable <u>nodules</u> or if there is clinical suspicion of <u>malignancy</u>

* Assess each <u>nodule</u> individually for risk features.





| <br><u>Sonographic</u> evaluation of <u>thyroid</u> <u>nodules</u> [[6]](/library/Um0bUg)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <br>Overview<br> | Risk pattern | <u>Ultrasound</u> findings |
| <br>Sonographic signs of thyroid malignancy<br> | High risk | <br>* Solid <u>hypoechoic</u> <u>nodule</u> or solid <u>hypoechoic</u> component with at least one of the following:<br><br>* Irregular margins<br><br>* Taller-than-wide shape<br><br>* Microcalcifications<br><br>* Rim calcifications with extruding tissue<br><br>* Extrathyroidal extension<br><br> |
| Intermediate risk | <br>* Solid <u>hypoechoic</u> <u>nodule</u> without high-risk features<br><br> |  |
| <br>Sonographic signs of benign thyroid nodules<br> | Low risk | <br><br>* <u>Isoechoic</u> or <u>hyperechoic</u> solid <u>nodule</u><br><br>* Cystic <u>nodule</u> with eccentric solid component<br><br><br> |
| Very low risk | <br><br>* Partially cystic <u>nodule</u><br><br>* Spongiform <u>nodule</u><br><br><br> |  |
| Benign | <br>* Cystic <u>nodules</u> (<u>anechoic</u>) without solid component<br><br> |  |





> [!TIP]
> <u>Thyroid ultrasound</u> is not a <u>screening test</u> for the general population. It is indicated as initial test for patients with palpable <u>thyroid</u> <u>nodules</u> or clinical suspicion for <u>thyroid malignancy</u>. [[3]](/library/70X4h9)




> [!TIP]
> Solid, <u>hypoechoic</u> <u>nodules</u> with irregular margins, microcalcifications, taller-than-wide shape, extrathyroidal growth, and/or <u>cervical lymphadenopathy</u> should raise suspicion for <u>malignancy</u> and require further evaluation with <u>FNAC</u>.

### Subsequent evaluation




#### <u>Thyroid scintigraphy</u> [[3]](/library/70X4h9)[[10]](/library/8zaOuM)




* Indication: <u>thyroid</u> <u>nodule</u>(s) in a patient with low <u>TSH</u>

* Contraindications: pregnant and <u>breastfeeding</u> women

* Findings and interpretation

* <u>Cold nodule</u> (hypofunctioning <u>nodule</u>): Evaluate for <u>indications for FNAC of thyroid nodules</u> with <u>ultrasound</u>.

* <u>Hot nodule</u> (hyperfunctioning <u>nodule</u>): rarely malignant, <u>FNAC</u> not recommended [[11]](/library/sfXtnx)

* Solitary <u>hot nodule</u>: <u>toxic adenoma</u>

* Multiple <u>hot nodules</u>: <u>toxic multinodular goiter</u>  [[12]](/library/no07cS)





![Thyroid scintigraphy](media/riwo5p37q47dmr4mc8ilyngp.jpg)

Thyroid scintigraphy

![Thyroid scan hot nodule](media/pdpud9wj0rynjzixazcykqat.jpg)

Thyroid scan hot nodule

![Cold nodule on thyroid scintigraphy](media/joqpph3gwz7oip3gjqvpph1x.jpg)

Cold nodule on thyroid scintigraphy




> [!TIP]
> <u>Malignancy</u> is rare in hyperfunctioning (hot) <u>nodules</u>. [[11]](/library/sfXtnx)




#### <u>Fine-needle aspiration cytology</u> (<u>FNAC</u>) [[3]](/library/70X4h9)[[6]](/library/Um0bUg)




* Indications for FNAC of thyroid nodules

* Solid <u>hypoechoic</u> <u>nodules</u> ≥ 1 cm with/without additional <u>sonographic signs of thyroid cancer</u>

* Consider for solid <u>hypoechoic</u> <u>nodules</u> < 1 cm if any of the following are present: 

* Extrathyroidal growth

* <u>Cervical lymphadenopathy</u>

* Symptoms suggestive of distant <u>metastases</u>

* Patient preference for <u>FNAC</u> over observation

* Partly cystic, <u>isoechoic</u>, and <u>hyperechoic</u> <u>nodules</u> ≥ 1.5 cm (low-risk pattern)

* Consider in spongiform or partly cystic <u>nodule</u> ≥ 2 cm (very low-risk pattern).

* Procedure

* <u>Thyroid</u> cells are obtained using a fine (e.g., 25-gauge) needle, and then observed under a microscope.  [[3]](/library/70X4h9)

* Multiple <u>nodules</u> may require <u>FNAC</u> depending on their <u>sonographic</u> appearance.

* Findings: categorized according to the <u>Bethesda system for thyroid cytopathology</u>





> [!TIP]
> If <u>thyroid scintigraphy</u> is performed, <u>sonographic</u> features of <u>thyroid</u> <u>nodules</u> should be used to determine which <u>cold nodules</u> require <u>FNAC</u>. <u>Cold nodules</u> with a benign appearance on <u>thyroid ultrasound</u> do not routinely require <u>FNAC</u>.




| <br>Bethesda system for thyroid cytopathology [[13]](/library/bdXHoC)<br> |  |
| --- | --- |
| Diagnostic category | <br>Management [[6]](/library/Um0bUg)<br> |
| I: Nondiagnostic or unsatisfactory | <br><br>* Repeat <u>FNAC</u> under <u>ultrasound</u> guidance.<br><br>* Consider <u>surgery</u> if any of the following are present:<br><br>* High risk category on <u>ultrasound</u><br><br>* <u>Red flags for thyroid cancer</u><br><br>* Increased size of the <u>nodule</u> on follow-up scan<br><br><br> |
| II: Benign | <br><br>* No further immediate diagnostic tests required<br><br>* Repeat <u>FNAC</u> or <u>sonography</u> within 1– 2 years depending on <u>sonographic</u> features.<br><br>* After two benign findings, no further follow-up is needed.<br><br>* If there is an increase in size or the size is > 4 cm: Consider surgical removal for symptom relief.<br><br><br> |
| III: <u>Atypia</u> or follicular lesion of undetermined significance | <br>* Consider any of the following:<br><br>* Repeat <u>FNAC</u> under <u>ultrasound</u> guidance.<br><br>* Molecular testing<br><br>* Surveillance or <u>thyroid lobectomy</u> with histopathological examination of the resected <u>nodule</u><br><br> |
| IV: Follicular <u>neoplasm</u> or suspicious for follicular <u>neoplasm</u> | <br>* Molecular testing or <u>thyroid lobectomy</u> (see “<u>Follicular adenoma</u>” for details)<br><br> |
| V: Suspicious for <u>malignancy</u> | <br>* See “<u>Thyroid cancer</u>.”<br><br> |
| VI: Malignant |  |

## Follicular adenoma

### <u>Epidemiology</u>




* <u>Follicular adenoma</u> is the most common type of <u>thyroid adenoma</u>. [[9]](/library/Dgb1xG)

* 10–15% of follicular <u>neoplasms</u> are malignant.





### Clinical features [[9]](/library/Dgb1xG)




* Often presents as a slow-growing solitary <u>nodule</u>

* Patients are typically <u>euthyroid</u>.

* In rare cases, patients can manifest with <u>clinical features of hyperthyroidism</u> (∼ 1% of follicular <u>adenomas</u> develop into toxic <u>adenomas</u>). [[14]](/library/zhXrgB)





### Diagnostics [[6]](/library/Um0bUg)




<u>Follicular adenoma</u> is a histopathological diagnosis. <u>Cytology</u> alone cannot distinguish between <u>adenoma</u> and <u>carcinoma</u>. For the initial workup, see “<u>Diagnostic approach to thyroid nodules</u>”.




* <u>Thyroid function tests</u>: <u>TSH</u> is typically normal.

* <u>Thyroid ultrasound</u>: may show <u>sonographic</u> signs of <u>malignancy</u> or appear benign

* <u>FNAC</u>

* Follicular <u>neoplasm</u> or follicular lesion of undetermined significance

* Cannot distinguish between <u>follicular adenoma</u> and <u>carcinoma</u>

* <u>Confirmatory test</u>

* Surgical excision (e.g., <u>hemithyroidectomy</u>) with histologic analysis  [[7]](/library/5XXiA9)[[9]](/library/Dgb1xG)

* Findings: normal follicular structure with no <u>tumor</u> invasion into the surrounding tissues (e.g., capsule, <u>blood vessels</u>).





![Thyroid follicular adenoma](media/sluepoeedg4xg146d0fmqrqu.jpg)

Thyroid follicular adenoma




### Treatment [[9]](/library/Dgb1xG)




* <u>Thyroid surgery</u> is always indicated, both for definitive diagnosis and treatment.

* Initial surgical excision shows no evidence of cancer: no further treatment required

* If follicular cancer is identified on <u>histopathology</u>: completion <u>thyroidectomy</u> and adjuvant <u>treatment of thyroid cancer</u> as needed

---

## Toxic adenoma

### <u>Epidemiology</u>




* Third most common cause of <u>hyperthyroidism</u>

* Sex: <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u>  [[15]](/library/j3Y_RK)

* Age: more common in individuals 30–50 years of age





### Pathophysiology




* <u>Gain-of-function</u> mutations of <u>TSH receptor</u> <u>gene</u>;  in a single precursor cell → autonomous functioning of the <u>thyroid follicular cells</u> of a single <u>nodule</u>  → focal <u>hyperplasia</u> of <u>thyroid</u> follicular cells → <u>toxic adenoma</u>

* The autonomous thyroid nodule overproduces <u>thyroid</u> <u>hormones</u> → <u>hyperthyroidism</u> → decrease in <u>pituitary</u> <u>TSH</u> secretion → suppression of <u>hormone</u> production in the rest of the gland





### Clinical features




* Palpable, usually painless <u>nodule</u> in otherwise normal gland

* <u>Symptoms of thyrotoxicosis</u>





### Diagnostics [[16]](/library/8HbOHE)




For the initial workup, see “<u>Diagnostic approach to thyroid nodules</u>.”




* <u>Thyroid function tests</u>: : ↑ T3 and ↓ <u>TSH</u>

* <u>Thyroid ultrasound</u>: <u>sonographic signs of a benign thyroid nodule</u>; in some cases, increased <u>perfusion</u>

* <u>Thyroid scintigraphy</u>

* Solitary, <u>hot nodule</u>

* Suppression of rest of the gland

* <u>FNAC</u>: Indicated not as a <u>confirmatory test</u> for <u>toxic adenoma</u> but to identify <u>malignancy</u> in suspicious <u>nodules</u> (see “<u>Indications for FNAC of thyroid nodules</u>”)





### Treatment [[10]](/library/8zaOuM)




* Initial management: <u>treatment of hyperthyroidism</u>

* <u>Beta blockers</u> for symptom control

* <u>Antithyroid drugs</u> to achieve <u>euthyroidism</u>

* Definitive treatment options [[9]](/library/Dgb1xG)[[17]](/library/ZcXZaC)

* <u>Hemithyroidectomy</u> or isthmusectomy for a solitary <u>toxic adenoma</u>

* <u>Radioactive iodine ablation</u> (<u>RAIA</u>)  [[16]](/library/8HbOHE)

* Less invasive therapy (e.g., <u>ethanol ablation</u>, <u>radiofrequency ablation</u>, <u>laser ablation</u>) may be considered in patients who are neither candidates for <u>surgery</u> nor <u>RAIA</u>. [[16]](/library/8HbOHE)[[18]](/library/yoXde_)

---

## Toxic multinodular goiter

### <u>Epidemiology</u> [[16]](/library/8HbOHE)




* Sex: <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u>

* Age: often > 60 years

* Second most common cause of <u>hyperthyroidism</u>

* Develops in 10% of patients with a long-standing nodular <u>goiter</u>

* More prevalent in <u>iodine</u>-deficient regions





### Pathophysiology




* Chronic <u>iodine deficiency</u>/<u>thyroid</u> dysfunction → decreased <u>hormone</u> production → increased <u>hypothalamic</u> <u>TRH</u> secretion → persistent <u>TSH</u> stimulation of the <u>thyroid</u> gland → <u>hyperplasia</u> of <u>thyroid</u> <u>nodules</u>, some more active than others → multinodular <u>goiter</u> (nontoxic MNG)

* Multiple <u>somatic mutations</u> of <u>TSH receptor</u> occur in long-standing <u>goiters</u> (> 60% of cases) → autonomous functioning of some <u>nodules</u> (<u>toxic MNG</u>) → <u>hyperthyroidism</u> (due to ↑ release of both T3 and T4)





### Clinical features [[16]](/library/8HbOHE)




* Painless <u>goiter</u> with multiple palpable <u>nodules</u>

* Symptoms of <u>thyrotoxicosis</u>





### Diagnostics [[16]](/library/8HbOHE)




For the initial workup of a nodular <u>goiter</u>, see “<u>Diagnostic approach to thyroid nodules</u>.”




* <u>Thyroid function tests</u>: ↑ T3 and ↓ <u>TSH</u>

* <u>Thyroid ultrasound</u>: multiple <u>nodules</u> within the <u>thyroid</u> <u>parenchyma</u>; increased <u>perfusion</u>

* <u>Thyroid scintigraphy</u> [[12]](/library/no07cS)

* Increased <u>radioiodine uptake</u> by multiple hyperfunctioning (hot) <u>nodules</u>

* Decreased uptake (suppression) by the rest of the gland and intervening <u>parenchyma</u>

* Hypofunctioning or <u>cold nodules</u> may also be present in the multinodular gland.

* <u>FNAC</u>: not routinely required (see “<u>Indications for FNAC of thyroid nodules</u>”)

* <u>Histopathology</u> of resected tissue: patches of enlarged follicular cells distended with colloid and with flattened <u>epithelium</u>





### Treatment [[10]](/library/8zaOuM)[[17]](/library/ZcXZaC)




* Initial management: <u>treatment of hyperthyroidism</u>

* <u>Beta blockers</u> for symptom control

* <u>Antithyroid drugs</u> to achieve <u>euthyroidism</u>

* Definitive treatment options [[9]](/library/Dgb1xG)

* <u>Total thyroidectomy</u> or <u>near-total thyroidectomy</u>

* <u>Radioactive iodine ablation</u>

---

## Thyroid cysts

### Classification and etiology [[7]](/library/5XXiA9)




* Simple cysts are exclusively fluid-filled <u>nodules</u> lined by benign <u>epithelial</u> cells.

* Complex cysts are partly solid and partly cystic and carry a 5–10% risk of <u>malignancy</u>.  [[19]](/library/fC0krR)

* Most commonly due to cystic degeneration of <u>thyroid</u> tissue or <u>involution</u> of an <u>adenoma</u>





### Clinical features




* Palpable <u>thyroid</u> <u>nodule</u>

* Hemorrhage into a cyst → <u>pain</u> and rapid enlargement of the <u>nodule</u>

* A large cyst or extensive hemorrhage can cause compression symptoms (e.g., <u>hoarseness</u>, <u>dysphagia</u>).





### Diagnostics [[6]](/library/Um0bUg)




The initial workup is the same as that for other <u>thyroid</u> <u>nodules</u> (see “<u>Diagnostic approach to thyroid nodules</u>”).




* <u>Thyroid function tests</u>: typically normal

* <u>Thyroid ultrasound</u>

* Cystic components appear <u>anechoic</u>.

* May be mixed with solid components

* <u>FNAC</u>: based on <u>FNAC</u> indications for <u>thyroid</u> <u>nodules</u> [[6]](/library/Um0bUg)[[20]](/library/sTbtHG)

* Purely cystic <u>nodule</u>: diagnostic <u>FNAC</u> not recommended

* Partly cystic <u>nodule</u> 

* Low risk pattern (eccentric solid component): <u>FNAC</u> if size is ≥ 1.5 cm

* Very low risk pattern: Consider <u>FNAC</u> if size is ≥ 2 cm.





### Treatment [[6]](/library/Um0bUg)




* Benign cysts 

* Asymptomatic cysts: observation

* Large or symptomatic cysts (or patient preference)

* <u>Aspiration</u> with/without <u>ethanol ablation</u>  [[21]](/library/WdXPKC)

* <u>Surgery</u> may be considered if <u>aspiration</u> is not effective.

* Malignant cysts: See “<u>Thyroid cancer</u>.”

---

## Special patient groups

### Pregnant patients [[3]](/library/70X4h9)




Management of <u>thyroid</u> <u>nodules</u> in <u>pregnancy</u> is similar to those in nonpregnant patients, except for the following points.




* Diagnostics

* In patients with low <u>TSH</u>, <u>thyroid scintigraphy</u> should be deferred until after <u>pregnancy</u> and cessation of <u>breastfeeding</u>.

* Newly symptomatic or growing <u>thyroid</u> <u>nodules</u> should be followed up with <u>thyroid ultrasound</u>.

* <u>FNAC</u> may be safely performed during <u>pregnancy</u> if indicated.

* Treatment

* <u>RAIA</u> is contraindicated during <u>pregnancy</u> and <u>breastfeeding</u>.

* If <u>thyroid cancer</u> is suspected or diagnosed during <u>pregnancy</u>:

* Postpone <u>surgery</u> until after the <u>pregnancy</u>, unless there are signs of aggressive cancer or advanced growth; <u>surgery</u> is relatively safe during the <u>second trimester</u>.

* If <u>surgery</u> is deferred, consider administration of <u>levothyroxine</u> to maintain <u>TSH</u> at low to normal levels.





### Children [[3]](/library/70X4h9)




* Management is similar to that of <u>thyroid</u> <u>nodules</u> in adults.

* <u>Thyroid</u> <u>nodules</u> in children are more frequently malignant.

---
